title: The Day I Became a Team Leader
script: Narrator: [warmly] Last month, my manager called me into her office, and I thought I was in trouble because that almost never happens.
Narrator: Instead, she told me I was going to become the new team leader for the marketing group. I was so surprised that I forgot to say thank you.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I had worked at that company for three years, but I never expected a promotion so soon, especially because two coworkers had been there longer than me.
Narrator: When I told my colleagues, some of them were happy for me, but I could feel that others felt a little strange about it.
Narrator: [carefully] My first week as a leader was harder than I expected, because I had to give tasks to people who used to be my equals.
Narrator: One coworker, Budi, seemed distant at first. He barely spoke to me during meetings, although we used to eat lunch together every day.
Narrator: [reflective] So one afternoon, I asked him directly if something was wrong. He admitted that he had wanted the position too, and he needed some time to accept it.

Narrator: I acknowledged his disappointment without asking him to praise the decision. We discussed his role, my expectations, and how his experience could contribute without making him responsible for my success.
Narrator: [honestly] After that conversation, things slowly improved between us, because we finally spoke honestly instead of avoiding each other.
Narrator: I learned that leadership isn't about being liked immediately. It's about listening carefully, even when a conversation feels uncomfortable.
Narrator: [gently] Now I ask for relevant input, state who decides, use clear criteria, and explain choices. Listening does not remove my responsibility to decide on time.
Narrator: Budi and I have lunch together again, and he recently helped me train a new employee, which meant a lot to me.
Narrator: [encouraging] I document key decisions, invite private and written feedback, and correct mistakes openly. I also ask my manager for coaching when the new authority feels unclear.
Narrator: If someone had told me a year ago that I would lead this team, I probably wouldn't have believed them.
Narrator: [sincere] But here I am, and although it's difficult sometimes, I'm proud of how far I've come since that nervous day in my manager's office.

She had made a big mistake
quiz.explanation: She says her manager almost never calls her in, so she assumed something was wrong.

quiz.explanation: Budi admitted he had wanted the leadership position and needed time to accept the change.

quiz.explanation: She now asks for everyone's opinion before making important decisions.

quiz.explanation: Budi recently helped her train a new employee, which meant a lot to her.

quiz.explanation: His behavior follows an unspoken disappointment.

options: Praise the selection or hide his disappointment
quiz.explanation: Professional conduct does not require false emotion.

options: Assign work using visible criteria and document important decisions

options: The leader must listen, explain, and still own timely decisions
quiz.explanation: Consultation has a purpose and a responsible decision-maker.

options: Budi contributes to training and their work communication becomes normal
quiz.explanation: Cooperation returns without pretending disappointment vanished.

qualityReview.scriptDecision: revise; turn personal tension into fair leadership through criteria, role clarity, private discussion, and accountable decisions

title: Deciding Whether the App Is Ready to Launch
script: Sari: [seriously] Bayu, yesterday’s test found a login crash and a payment record that sometimes fails to save. I recommend stopping the October launch.
Bayu: Those are serious. Do we know how often they occur or which users are affected?
Sari: [carefully] Not yet. We reproduced both problems, but we need logs and a wider test to understand the scope.
Bayu: Then we should not promise a new date before the technical team estimates the work.
Sari: Agreed. The payment issue is a release blocker. We must also check whether wrong data was stored and whether privacy or security is affected.
Bayu: [thoughtful] Who will own each investigation?
Sari: The login lead will study the crash. The payment lead and security reviewer will examine the transaction flow. I will coordinate testing and evidence.
Bayu: What should we tell clients today?
Sari: [honestly] State that testing found issues that could affect login and payment reliability, so the launch is paused. Explain the impact and give a time for the next update.
Bayu: We should avoid blaming developers or giving technical guesses that may change.
Sari: Yes. We can apologize for the disruption and help clients adjust any connected plans.
Bayu: [reflective] What conditions must be met before release?
Sari: Root causes understood, fixes reviewed, payment records checked, important tests passed, and responsible owners accepting any remaining documented risk.
Bayu: Should we focus the whole team on only these two defects?
Sari: Not automatically. The technical leads should protect urgent work while maintaining necessary support and review. Rushing everyone can create new errors.
Bayu: [encouraging] I will draft the client notice. You prepare the issue owners, test criteria, and tomorrow’s update meeting.
Sari: I will also preserve test evidence and use non-sensitive data in shared reports.
Bayu: Good. The previous early launch taught us that a date is not more important than a reliable product.
Sari: [relieved] Once we have evidence, we can publish a realistic plan rather than replacing one weak promise with another.
Bayu: Agreed. Pause, investigate, communicate, fix, and verify before we release.

A price increase and broken phone
quiz.explanation: Both affect core customer actions.

quiz.explanation: Investigation must also protect data.

quiz.question: What should they check besides visible failure?
options: Whether incorrect data was stored and whether security or privacy is affected

options: A factual notice, impact on their plans, and the next confirmed update time
quiz.explanation: Communication distinguishes known facts from estimates.

quiz.question: What allows release later?
options: Fixes pass defined tests and responsible owners accept the remaining risk
quiz.explanation: Quality gates rather than the calendar decide readiness.

qualityReview.scriptDecision: replace; treat payment failure as a release blocker requiring severity review, data checks, ownership, retesting, and evidence-based scheduling

title: Working From Home: What I Learned
script: Narrator: [warmly] When my company allowed remote work last year, I was thrilled, because I imagined lazy mornings and complete freedom.
Narrator: The reality looked quite different. During my first week, I worked in pajamas until three in the afternoon, and I felt strangely unproductive.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Without my usual office routine, my days started blending together, and I often forgot which day of the week it actually was.
Narrator: I also missed something I never expected to miss, which was simply talking to my coworkers during small breaks.
Narrator: [carefully] At home, I sometimes went a whole day without speaking to another human being, and that made me feel isolated.
Narrator: So I decided to change a few habits, even though it felt awkward to create new rules just for myself.
Narrator: [reflective] First, I chose a morning routine that marked the start of work. Getting dressed helped me, although another person may need a different cue.
Narrator: It sounds small, but it helped my brain understand that work time had officially begun.
Narrator: [honestly] Second, our team offered short optional check-ins and written channels. We considered time zones, access needs, and people who did not want extra video calls.
Narrator: Those calls became the highlight of my day, because they reminded me that we were still a team, although we worked apart.
Narrator: [gently] Third, my manager clarified response hours and emergency channels. I set an ending time, took breaks, and requested equipment advice for a safer workspace.
Narrator: After six I closed routine work. A true urgent issue used the agreed channel; ordinary messages waited until the next work period.
Narrator: [encouraging] These changes seem simple, but together they turned a confusing situation into something I genuinely enjoy now.
Narrator: I still miss office life sometimes, especially the coffee machine conversations, but I've finally found a rhythm that works for me.
Narrator: [sincere] If remote work is difficult, discuss workload and support rather than blaming yourself. If isolation, pain, or distress continues, seek appropriate professional help.

quiz.explanation: The habit is personal, not a universal rule.

options: Optional and scheduled with teammates’ availability and preferences
quiz.explanation: Connection should not add pressure.

quiz.explanation: Remote work design is not only an individual duty.

quiz.explanation: Persistent health effects need appropriate support.

qualityReview.scriptDecision: revise; share responsibility between worker and employer for boundaries, communication, accessibility, and a safe workspace

title: A Job Interview That Changed My Mind
script: Interviewer: [warmly] Thank you for coming in today, Dimas. Please, sit down and make yourself comfortable.
Candidate: Thank you for having me. I'll admit, I'm a little nervous, since this is my first interview in years.
Interviewer: [thoughtful] That's completely understandable. Take a breath, and let's just have a normal conversation, not an interrogation.
Candidate: That helps, thank you. I appreciate you saying that.
Interviewer: [carefully] So, tell me, why did you decide to apply for this position, especially after working at the same company for six years?
Candidate: Honestly, I loved my old job for a long time, but recently I stopped growing there. I wanted a new challenge.
Interviewer: [reflective] What kind of challenge are you hoping to find here specifically?
Candidate: I want to work on bigger projects, and I want to learn from a team that pushes me to improve.
Interviewer: [honestly] That's exactly the environment we try to create here. Can you describe a difficult situation you handled well?
Candidate: Once, a major client threatened to leave because of a mistake my team made. I called them personally and fixed it within two days.
Interviewer: [gently] That's a strong example. How did you feel during that stressful situation?
Candidate: Terrified, if I'm being completely truthful. But I focused on solving the problem instead of worrying about how it looked.
Interviewer: [encouraging] I appreciate your honesty. Many candidates pretend they never feel stressed, which frankly isn't believable.
Candidate: I don't think anyone truly enjoys those moments, but they do teach you a lot about yourself.
Interviewer: [sincere] Well, Dimas, I think this conversation has been genuinely refreshing. Do you have any questions for me before we finish?
Candidate: Yes, actually. What do you personally enjoy most about working here?
Interviewer: Honestly, the people. Even during hard weeks, this team supports each other, which isn't always common in this industry.
Candidate: That's exactly what I was hoping to hear. Thank you again for this opportunity, and for making me feel so relaxed today.

quiz.explanation: Dimas admits he's nervous because it's his first interview in years.

options: Specific examples of support, management, workload, and role terms
quiz.explanation: One person’s view is useful but not complete evidence.

qualityReview.scriptDecision: keep; realistic interview dialogue shows nerves, behavioral evidence, honest emotion, and a candidate asking about workplace experience

title: My Worst Meeting Ever
script: Narrator: [warmly] I want to tell you about the worst meeting of my career, because looking back now, it's actually a little funny.
Narrator: It happened during my second month at a new company, when I still didn't know everyone's name.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I was presenting our quarterly numbers to the whole department, including the company's owner, who rarely attended these meetings.
Narrator: I had practiced my slides the night before, so I felt reasonably confident when I walked into the room that morning.
Narrator: [carefully] Then, halfway through my presentation, my laptop suddenly froze, and the screen showed my personal photos instead of the report.
Narrator: Everyone saw a photo of my cat wearing a tiny hat, right there on the big screen for the whole department.
Narrator: [reflective] My face turned bright red, and for a moment, I genuinely considered running out of the room and never coming back.
Narrator: Instead, I took a breath, closed the photo app, and said, well, at least you know I have excellent taste in hats.
Narrator: [honestly] To my surprise, the room actually laughed, and even the owner smiled, which helped me relax immediately.
Narrator: I finished the presentation. Afterward, I checked what had appeared and confirmed that no client, document, or sensitive personal image had been exposed.
Narrator: [gently] Before that day, I believed a perfect presentation meant a flawless one, without any mistakes whatsoever.
Narrator: Now I value a calm recovery, but humor does not remove a privacy incident. A mistake should also improve the next process.
Narrator: [encouraging] A coworker named Rani, who I barely knew then, came up afterward and said my reaction actually calmed her own nerves for later meetings.
Narrator: Rani later helped me test a safer setup: a work profile, closed personal apps, hidden notification previews, and only the presentation window shared.
Narrator: [sincere] I can laugh about the harmless cat image now, but the real lesson is to recover respectfully, check the impact, and prevent a more serious exposure next time.

quiz.explanation: It happened during her second month at a new company.

quiz.explanation: A photo of her cat wearing a tiny hat appeared instead of the report.

quiz.explanation: She joked, saying at least everyone knew she had excellent taste in hats.

options: That her reaction calmed Rani's own nerves for later meetings
quiz.explanation: Rani said the narrator's calm reaction helped calm her own nerves for future meetings.

quiz.question: What lesson does the narrator take from this experience?
options: People remember how you handle awkward moments more than perfection
quiz.explanation: She learns that people remember how you handle an awkward moment more than perfection.

quiz.question: What creates the embarrassing moment?
options: Personal photos appear on the presentation screen
quiz.explanation: The display exposes unrelated private content.

quiz.question: How does the narrator recover in the room?
options: Close the photo app, acknowledge the interruption briefly, and continue
quiz.explanation: A calm response limits disruption.

quiz.question: What should happen after the meeting?
options: Check what was exposed and report any sensitive incident through policy
quiz.explanation: Humor does not replace incident review.

quiz.question: How does the narrator prevent a repeat?
options: Use a work profile, close apps, disable previews, and test the display
quiz.explanation: Technical preparation protects private and work data.

quiz.question: What is the revised lesson?
options: Recover calmly, then improve the system instead of romanticizing every mistake
Personal devices should have no security
quiz.explanation: Resilience includes prevention and accountability.

qualityReview.scriptDecision: revise; retain humor while treating exposed personal media as a privacy and device-separation incident

title: A Performance Review With a Clear Growth Plan
script: Manager: [warmly] Ratih, this six-month review will cover results, support, and one development goal. You may ask for clarification at any point.
Ratih: Thank you. I prepared notes because review meetings make me nervous.
Manager: [thoughtful] Your completion rate improved, and client feedback says your responses are clearer and faster. The report shows the period and project types we measured.
Ratih: I am glad the new weekly planning system helped.
Manager: One area I want to understand is participation in planning meetings. You often send useful ideas afterward rather than during discussion.
Ratih: [honestly] I need time to organize my thoughts, and fast group conversations make me worry that an unfinished idea will sound careless.
Manager: That is useful context. The goal is not speaking for its own sake. We need your knowledge before decisions close.
Ratih: Could agendas include the main questions earlier?
Manager: [encouraging] Yes. I will send decision questions one day ahead where possible. You can add written input before the meeting.
Ratih: I would also like the chair to invite me on the topic I prepared, rather than expecting me to interrupt.
Manager: That is reasonable. For urgent or safety-related claims, bring evidence or say what still needs checking. We will not use an arbitrary rule such as speaking when “seventy percent sure.”
Ratih: [reflective] What would improvement look like over the next month?
Manager: Contribute to two relevant planning decisions, verbally or in writing, and record what support helped. Quality matters more than a word count.
Ratih: Can we review it after four weeks instead of waiting six months?
Manager: [warmly] Yes. I also want feedback on whether the meeting format gives everyone a fair chance to contribute.
Ratih: Then the plan addresses both my skill and the team environment.
Manager: Exactly. Development should not mean forcing one communication style on every employee.
Ratih: [determined] I will prepare for tomorrow’s agenda and add one written question this afternoon.
Manager: Good. I will send you the performance data and our agreed actions so you can correct anything I recorded inaccurately.
Ratih: [sincere] Thank you. Specific evidence and a clear follow-up make the feedback feel useful, not vague.

quiz.explanation: Advice should fit risk and purpose.

options: Agenda questions, preparation time, written input, and an invited speaking point
quiz.explanation: Multiple channels reduce one narrow performance demand.

quiz.explanation: The plan uses behavior and timely support.

qualityReview.scriptDecision: replace; make feedback measurable and create safe contribution options instead of telling an employee to speak at seventy-percent certainty

title: Planning Pak Anton’s Modest Office Farewell
script: Nadia: [warmly] Yusuf, Pak Anton leaves on Friday. HR checked with him, and he is comfortable with a short farewell, not a large surprise.
Yusuf: Good. What did he say he would enjoy?
Nadia: Tea, simple food, and written messages from the team. He does not want a long speech or public video.
Yusuf: [thoughtful] Then we should respect that. How will food be arranged?
Nadia: We can order from an approved halal supplier and ask privately about allergies and other dietary needs. There should be suitable options, not only cake.
Yusuf: What about a gift? He often mentions gardening.
Nadia: [carefully] Let us not buy tools without asking. He may own them already, and some tools may not suit him. A general gift card from a suitable shop may give him choice.
Yusuf: We could collect money, but people may feel pressured at work.
Nadia: Contributions must be optional and private, with no minimum. The card is open to everyone even if they give no money.
Yusuf: [relieved] Good. Managers should not receive a list of who contributed.
Nadia: Agreed. We also need approval for the meeting-room time and clarity about whether company funds cover food.
Yusuf: If they do not, we keep the plan within voluntary personal contributions and do not use another project budget.
Nadia: [thoughtful] The gathering can begin at four and finish in thirty minutes so people with transport or care duties may leave on time.
Yusuf: Attendance should be optional too. We can send Pak Anton the written messages afterward.
Nadia: No music or embarrassing games. One short thank-you from the team, then time for appropriate conversation.
Yusuf: [encouraging] I will prepare an accessible digital card and a paper version. People can choose either format.
Nadia: I will confirm food, room access, and the approved budget. We should avoid sharing retirement details beyond what he has allowed.
Yusuf: That covers consent, privacy, food, time, and money.
Nadia: [sincere] A respectful goodbye should make him feel valued, not turn his last day into a performance he must manage.
Yusuf: Exactly. Simple, warm, and based on what he actually wants.

title: The Meeting I Declined With an Alternative
script: Narrator: [warmly] A project manager invited me to a planning meeting scheduled during the only two hours I had reserved for finishing a required report.
Narrator: My first reaction was to accept. In our office, declining a meeting can feel like saying the topic is unimportant.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Then I read the agenda. Only one item needed my technical input, and the remaining discussion concerned another team.
Narrator: I wrote to the manager that I could not attend the full hour without risking the report deadline.
Narrator: [carefully] Instead of stopping there, I offered three alternatives: answer the technical question in writing, join the first fifteen minutes, or speak with her before lunch.
Narrator: She chose a short call before lunch. We solved the question in twelve minutes, and she copied the decision into the meeting notes.
Narrator: [reflective] During the main meeting, the team could continue without waiting for me. I finished the report on time.
Narrator: The experience taught me that protecting focused work does not require ignoring colleagues.
Narrator: [honestly] A useful decline explains the conflict briefly and offers an option that still serves the shared goal.
Narrator: I did not describe every task on my calendar or claim that my work was more important than theirs.
Narrator: [gently] I also checked that I truly was not needed for a decision. Sometimes attendance is part of the job, even when the timing is inconvenient.
Narrator: Afterward, the manager added “required decision-makers” beside each agenda item. Other invited people could decide whether their presence was useful.
Narrator: [encouraging] Our meeting attendance became smaller, and written updates became more common.
Narrator: Saying yes to every invitation had made me look available while quietly delaying promised work.
Narrator: [sincere] Now I respond based on purpose, role, and deadlines. A respectful no with a workable alternative can be more reliable than an automatic yes.

quiz.explanation: A focused alternative preserves coordination.

quiz.explanation: Boundary-setting still recognizes job duties.

quiz.explanation: Role clarity lets invitees judge usefully.

qualityReview.scriptDecision: keep; strong boundary-setting case links role, agenda, focused work, alternatives, and honest availability

title: Training the Person Who Would Replace Me
script: Narrator: [warmly] When I learned that I would move to another department, my manager asked me to train Rafi to handle the weekly inventory report.
Narrator: At first, I planned to show him the spreadsheet once and send my old notes. I had done the task for two years and forgot how many steps were not written down.
Narrator: [thoughtful] During our first session, Rafi asked why one supplier's numbers were always checked separately. The reason existed only in my memory.
Narrator: We created a clearer guide together. It included the source files, order of checks, common errors, deadline, and person to contact for unusual cases.
Narrator: [carefully] I demonstrated one report while explaining my decisions. The next week, Rafi completed it while I watched silently.
Narrator: He made one mistake with returned items. Instead of taking the keyboard, I asked him to trace the total back to the source.
Narrator: [reflective] He found the problem and added a warning to the guide in his own words.
Narrator: For the third report, I reviewed only the final figures and questions. Rafi no longer needed me beside him.
Narrator: [honestly] We also asked another coworker to follow the guide. She found two instructions that were obvious to us but unclear to a new reader.
Narrator: Before my transfer, Rafi handled the full cycle and sent the report on time.
Narrator: [gently] Training did not mean proving that the task was difficult or showing every shortcut at once. It meant making another person safely independent.
Narrator: I kept access rules in place. Rafi received the accounts required for his role; I did not share my personal password.
Narrator: [encouraging] The manager stored the guide in a team folder with an owner and review date, so it would not become an old forgotten file.
Narrator: On my first day in the new department, nobody called me about inventory. That silence was evidence of a successful handover.
Narrator: [sincere] Good knowledge transfer leaves a process stronger than one person's memory.

quiz.question: What task would Rafi take over?
quiz.explanation: The narrator was transferring a repeated reporting duty.

quiz.question: What weakness appeared in the old process?
options: Important reasons existed only in memory
quiz.explanation: Two years of habit had hidden unwritten knowledge.

quiz.question: How did Rafi learn after the demonstration?
options: He completed a report while the narrator observed
quiz.explanation: Practice gradually shifted responsibility.

quiz.question: Why did another coworker test the guide?
options: To find instructions unclear to new readers
quiz.explanation: A fresh reader revealed hidden assumptions.

quiz.question: What shows a successful handover?
options: The old worker stays necessary forever
The process works independently and safely
Only one person understands the task
quiz.explanation: Strong transfer reduces dependence on personal memory.

quiz.question: What hidden weakness does Rafi’s question reveal?
options: An important supplier check exists only in one person’s memory
The deadline is unknown to everyone
quiz.explanation: Undocumented knowledge creates dependence.

quiz.question: Why does the narrator avoid taking the keyboard?
options: Tracing the error helps Rafi learn the process independently
quiz.explanation: Guided practice builds diagnostic skill.

quiz.question: What does the third-party test reveal?
options: The report total is always wrong
Instructions obvious to the writers can confuse a new reader
quiz.explanation: Fresh users expose assumptions.

quiz.question: Why not share a personal password?
options: Role-based access should be granted through proper accounts
quiz.explanation: Handover must preserve security.

quiz.question: What keeps the guide useful later?
options: A team owner and scheduled review date
quiz.explanation: Documentation needs maintenance responsibility.

qualityReview.scriptDecision: keep; excellent knowledge-transfer story uses demonstration, practice, feedback, least privilege, ownership, and review dates

title: Correcting the Customer Without Winning an Argument
script: Laila: [warmly] Ms. Laila, your invoice charges us for delivery, but your salesperson promised free delivery.
Mr. Budi: Thank you for telling me. Do you have the quotation or message where that was stated?
Laila: [thoughtful] Yes, here is the email. It says delivery is included for orders above ten boxes.
Mr. Budi: I see that. Your order has eight boxes, so the automatic invoice added the normal fee.
Laila: [carefully] The salesperson knew we were ordering eight. He still told me there would be no charge.
Mr. Budi: Let me check the earlier message in the thread. Please give me a moment.
Laila: [reflective] Of course. I do not want to pay a fee that appeared after we agreed.
Mr. Budi: I found his message. You are correct: he specifically offered free delivery for this first order.
Laila: [honestly] Then the invoice should be changed.
Mr. Budi: Yes. I will remove the fee and send a corrected invoice today. I apologize for the inconsistency.
Laila: [gently] Thank you. I was worried you would only repeat the general policy.
Mr. Budi: The policy explains why the system added the fee, but it does not cancel a written promise made to you.
Laila: [encouraging] How will we avoid this on the next order?
Mr. Budi: I will add the standard threshold to your account note. Any exception must also appear clearly in the quotation before approval.
Laila: [sincere] That is fair. We may order more than ten boxes next time anyway.
Mr. Budi: I will also speak privately with the salesperson so special offers are entered into the billing system.
Laila: I appreciate that you checked the evidence instead of treating my complaint as an attack.
Mr. Budi: And I appreciate that you brought the email. The goal is an accurate invoice, not winning an argument.
Laila: Please send the correction to both me and our finance address.
Mr. Budi: I will. You should receive it within one hour, with the original invoice marked as canceled.

quiz.question: What fee does Mr. Budi question?
quiz.explanation: He expected delivery to be free.

quiz.question: What is the normal free-delivery rule?
quiz.explanation: The automated invoice followed a quantity threshold.

quiz.question: What evidence changes the result?
quiz.explanation: The email clearly offered an exception.

quiz.question: How will future exceptions be handled?
options: Written in quotations and billing records
quiz.explanation: Clear records align sales and billing.

quiz.question: What approach resolves the complaint?
options: Check evidence and correct the invoice without defensiveness
quiz.explanation: Accuracy is treated as the shared goal.

quiz.question: Why does the normal system add delivery?
options: The order has eight boxes, below the standard threshold
quiz.explanation: The rule explains the automated result.

quiz.question: What changes the correct outcome?
options: The next order may be larger
A written offer specifically promises free delivery for this order
quiz.explanation: Case-specific evidence overrides the general assumption.

quiz.question: Why is the policy still useful?
options: It proves the customer is wrong
It explains the system behavior even though it cannot cancel the exception
quiz.explanation: A cause and a contractual result can differ.

quiz.question: How will the company prevent repetition?
options: Record standard thresholds and approved exceptions in quotation and billing systems
Ask customers to remember every promise
quiz.explanation: Aligned records reduce billing conflict.

quiz.question: What closes the correction clearly?
options: A new invoice is sent and the original is marked canceled
quiz.explanation: Document status prevents duplicate or uncertain payment.

qualityReview.scriptDecision: keep; strong complaint-resolution dialogue distinguishes policy from a documented exception and repairs both invoice and process
